commentary.bottom_line: One small simulated trial in 72 surgical residents found that structured training on how to query and check a large language model raised decision quality scores (16.2 vs 13.5), and a pre-post study of 139 medical students found higher self-rated evaluation skill that was not objectively measured. No study tested training on override, escalation, or intervention points in agentic workflows, and none measured patient outcomes in practice.

perspectives.view: Two studies test training. The randomized trial is small, simulated, and uses a decision-quality score rather than patient outcomes. The pre-post study has no comparator and measures self-perception. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low. Neither study addresses override, escalation, or agentic workflows, which make up much of the recommendation.

Two hazard studies show that the skill gap exists. Medical students scored 0.41 of 3 on verifying AI outputs. A failure mode analysis of 86 modes ranked human error first and inadequate training second among high-risk modes. In the trial, trained residents solicited more evidence per case (3.0 vs 0.7), which may reflect checking behavior that intercepts errors.

Both tests took place offline with trainees, so fidelity and retention in live clinical workflows remain unmeasured. The trial attributes 88% of the improvement to changes in how residents interacted with the model. This suggests that training on the interaction process may carry the effect. Neither study reported training time or burden.

Both tests used trainees and simulated tasks, one in Taiwan and one in an unreported setting, and neither described the patient populations represented. No study examined whether trained clinicians detect AI errors in documentation or advice for patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

commentary.research_gap: Trials in practicing clinicians within live workflows should test whether training on verification, override, escalation, and agentic intervention points reduces errors that reach patients. These trials should use objective verification measures, follow users long enough to assess retention, and report training time and cost.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both used simulated tasks with trainees. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume the reported gains will transfer and would need to evaluate training effects locally.
